newsitem.title: UK: Dollar sticks to gains at end of energetic week.
newsitem.headline: Dollar sticks to gains at end of energetic week.

text.p: It was almost as if the dollar was leading a charmed life this week.
The currency's latest rally has seen it post a fresh multi-year high against the yen nearly every day this week -- the sole exception being Friday -- and a 37-month high against the mark on Thursday.

Adding to dollar bulls' underlying theme of health of the American economy and expectations of an interest rate rise there was relief over easing U.S.-Japan trade tensions and increasing expectations that European economic and monetary union would go ahead on time.
The dollar has risen by 3.7 percent against the yen and 3.8 percent on the mark since the rally started late last week.

It was at 1.7195 marks in late European trade on Friday, compared with 1.7198 a day earlier and its 37-month high of 1.7272. The dollar/yen rate was at 126.15, well short of the 56-month high of 127.19 yen it reached on Thursday but up from late Thursday's 126.03.
The currency's rally was triggered by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's visit to Asia late last week.

While in Tokyo Rubin expressed concern over Japan's swelling, and politically sensitive, trade surplus with the United States but also said currencies should not be used as instruments of trade policy.
A drop in the dollar/yen rate would make it more difficult for Japanese companies to export their goods to the U.S. market, as this would boost the prices of their goods in terms of dollars.

The dollar has risen steadily since then as dollar bulls took Rubin's trade comment as a green light, with the rally merely interrupted by top-level Japanese officials' increasingly explicit warnings about driving the yen down further.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said on Thursday that the yen's recent moves were excessive and that Japan would deal decisively with excessive currency moves. A ministry official said on Friday this was the Japanese government's official view.
The market was never very discouraged by such comments though they dented dollar sentiment temporarily.

"We've certainly seen lots of comments out of Japan indicating their willingness to do something... But it's still very uncertain at what level they will start to do something and what they will do," said Teis Knuthsen, international economist at First Chicago here.
Analysts have said there was little the Bank of Japan could do on its own to stem the dollar's rise and would need cooperation from the U.S. Federal Reserve for a lasting effect.

But this, they said, was highly unlikely, especially given Rubin's remarks on Thursday that a strong dollar was in the U.S. interest, although he tempered his comment by saying Washington shared Japan's concern over the yen's fall.

The dollar also found support from market optimism over European economic and monetary union (EMU), with prominent officials expressing enthusiasm over launching Europe's currency union on time in 1999.
EMU optimism dampens the mark as monetary union means replacing the mark with the euro, a currency considered to be less stable and credible.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said the EMU timetable must be maintained, EU commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said it was clear EMU would start on time with a significant number of countries, while Bank of France council member Paul Marchelli called for a broad-based EMU start including Italy, Spain and Portugal.

"Recent EMU developments are dollar-bullish, with the market looking more at a wider, softer EMU at this stage. It's already been reflected in the dollar/mark rally so far but it could still be bullish for the dollar," said Claudio Demolli, foreign exchange analyst at Merrill Lynch here.

Analysts said there was some room, though not much, left for the dollar to rise in this rally. The economic fundamentals supporting the dollar were still in place, but might be wearing thin, they said.
